overview: Hypsilophodon foxii was a small, fleet-footed ornithopod from the Early Cretaceous of southern England (~130–120 Ma), about two metres long. For over a century it was depicted as a tree-climber — based on a misinterpretation of its foot anatomy — before modern analysis confirmed it was a fast ground-runner. Dozens of individuals from a single site on the Isle of Wight suggest it lived or gathered in groups.

Hypsilophodon's self-sharpening, high-ridged cheek teeth gave it its name and allowed it to process a wide range of tough plant material. It coexisted with Baryonyx and Iguanodon in the Early Cretaceous Wessex ecosystem and represents the basal ornithopod body plan — bipedal, fast, medium-sized — that persisted from the Jurassic into the Cretaceous.

fossilSites.name: Wessex Formation
fossilSites.note: Barremian fluvial deposits with dozens of Hypsilophodon individuals from a single horizon, suggesting mass death or gregarious behaviour.

articles.title: The tree-climber myth
articles.body: Thomas Henry Huxley and John Hulke described Hypsilophodon in 1869. A 1974 paper by Galton proposed it could climb trees based on the reversed hallux (first toe) and grasping foot — citing parallels with modern tree-climbing birds. This interpretation was widely accepted until Biomechanical analysis in the 1970s–80s showed the foot anatomy was inconsistent with arboreal grasping. Modern analyses confirm Hypsilophodon was a fully terrestrial runner.

articles.title: Anatomy and locomotion
articles.body: Long hindlimbs relative to the body, a stiff tail and long lower leg segments indicate a fast runner. The self-sharpening ridged cheek teeth — which give the animal its name — processed vegetation by precise occlusion rather than the grinding batteries of hadrosaurs. The small size and agility would have been its primary defence against predators.

articles.title: Isle of Wight bonebed
articles.body: A single layer in the Wessex Formation on the Isle of Wight has yielded over 20 Hypsilophodon individuals of all ages. The cause of this accumulation — mass drowning, drought at a waterhole, or predator aggregation — is unknown, but the concentration confirms that Hypsilophodon occurred in social groups.

record.description: Hypsilophodon foxii was a small bipedal herbivorous ornithopod from the Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight. Numerous skulls and skeletons, many from a restricted locality, document a lightly built runner with a stiffened tail.
facts: The old idea that Hypsilophodon climbed trees is not supported by modern anatomy.
There is no bony body armour; supposed plates were misidentified material.
Its hands and feet are consistent with terrestrial bipedal locomotion.

review.ageReviewNote: The main Hypsilophodon bed is Barremian, close to 126-125 Ma.
